comments.value: As a thought, what about users who are sitting there and watching a video for a long period of time? I don't think you'd want to trigger AFK for them, and you don't want to force them to wiggle their mouse every few minutes, or have to set an option that they didn't have to set before. 🤔

@{5acad9ecc9dba010c9c3ec68|full_name}: I kinda left the definition of in-activity kinda vague specifically because of this. It's definitely not a simple suggestion. Even if you did something like say, check for microphone activity, that both excludes those who choose to play mute and can be accidentally circumvented by those who have overly sensitive microphones.
One might consider setting 'AFK time' in the settings menu at a default value of 'don't auto AFK', in order for the user to AFK or not on their own agency. I think everybody values the AFK function differently based on if they've made a custom animation for it or not. Additionally, the idea of making it its very own setting means that it can change with the user's context. This may fall into the definition of 'setting an option', however, so another concept.
To determine when to turn someone AFK or not, we should first have a definition for what 'activity' and 'inactivity' looks like in a way it's reasonable to measure. Some examples of in-activity could be:
-Keeping the Window out of focus is a good measure if someone is paying attention to the game. Best case scenario, the user has moved attention fully to something else, and most iffy scenario, the user may have tabbed over to another program for a short time. For example, going back and forth between blender/unity and the game to check how their avatar functions and what tweaks to make. Of course, currently, SteamVR overlay also triggers the animation, so it'd be a similar case as the current VR example.
-Far proximity from other users. A player not within a certain distance to another player is most likely not actually active. If a desktop is watching a video with a group of other players, it's still possible they're participating. Proximity to video players most likely won't work as a metric since every world is different and while some worlds have close up tv sized video players, others have far off movie theater sized video players.
Now, some things that I think are unambiguously activity.
-Moving is a certain way of proving the player is active, and I don't think I need to do any convincing there.
-Mic activity, as mentioned earlier, could be a bad option due to the presence of unusually sensitive microphones, and people who prefer to play mute. But in the case of push to talk, that press can be used as a definite way to ensure someone is currently active. If you want mic activity to be the deciding factor rather than just PTT, you could change how much mic activity is necessary to ward off the AFK state. Maybe little blips don't count, but full on seconds of activity do.
You could assign multiple cases of 'suggested inactivity' and have a different time threshold for each. Someone tabbing out for more than 10 seconds should be considered afk, Someone not moving, AND not speaking, AND not around anybody else can probably have a timer for 5 minutes. Somebody not moving, but with other people who are also active could probably have a much more generous limit, maybe 10-15 minutes. I personally find it hard to believe that someone could be in-game and unintentionally not move or speak at all for 10-15 minutes at a time to accidentally trigger the afk state, but if it's too much of a big deal, you could instead just have it so that the AFK state cannot be initiated while in proximity of one other 'active' player. Maybe put players in a 'soft AFK' state where the parameter doesn't change until they're out of proximity with other active players.
This turned into a wall of text fast, but in general, there's not real one single perfect solution to that problem you mention, but I think there's some reasonable workaround solutions.

@{5c4bd9bca31c1d6ef9355351|full_name}: For force afk, you could have a animation that go really slow then transfer to another state when not moving. That state set a bool to go in a duplicate afk branch that don't disable locomotion with a condition that detect if you move any velocity to get out.

details:
Currently, the AFK animation must be triggered manually by desktop players. For VR Players, afk happens naturally when the headset is removed or within the SteamVR Menu. Somebody who is unavailable in VR is unambiguously unavailable because they will trigger one of these two things.
However, Desktop players who don't hit the End key and abandon their keyboard will stare off into space indefinitely, the AFK animation never triggering, meaning that it's possible to appear standing, but not be actively playing or speaking.
title: [FEEDBACK] Auto-AFK desktop players after a period of In-activity
